speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The familiar signposts are fading, but the contours of a new global system have yet to take shape.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are in a period of transition – uncertain, unsettled and increasingly unstable.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are entering a new phase in global affairs – one that is more arbitrary, protectionist and dangerous.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For nearly 80 years since the end of World War II, America was the anchor for the free market economies of the world.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It championed free trade and open markets, and led efforts to build a multilateral trading system.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This World Trade Organization (WTO) system ushered in decades of global growth and stability.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It allowed trade to flourish and lifted millions out of poverty.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It benefited the world and contributed to America's own economic strength.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Objectively, America continues to enjoy unrivalled economic heft.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, the US rebounded more quickly than other advanced economies from the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It has surged ahead of all its major competitors in the advanced industrial world.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But not all Americans feel this way about their economy.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There are hollowed-out towns in what was once America's thriving industrial belt.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There are workers whose jobs have disappeared and whose incomes have stagnated.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They believe that the American economy is fundamentally broken.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Discontent was already visible in the 1990s when protestors disrupted the WTO meeting in Seattle.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Frustrations deepened following the Global Financial Crisis of 2008 and more recently, after the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To be clear, the global economic system is in need of reform.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Singapore and many others have called for changes, and we have been working with like-minded partners at the WTO to reform its processes.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A key concern in America is China – the sense that the US had given away too much in allowing China to join the WTO and that China competes on an unfair basis, for example, by heavily subsidising its own companies, putting up non-tariff barriers and restricting market access to US firms.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These concerns should be addressed within the WTO framework.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In particular, the trade arrangements and concessions made in the past when China was only 5% of the world's economy should be updated when China now makes up 15% of the world's gross domestic product (GDP).

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And if there are disagreements, they should be resolved through the WTO's dispute settlement system, which has been paralysed and urgently needs to be restored and reformed.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But what the US is doing now is not reform.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is rejecting the very system it created.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: According to the administration, the sweeping tariffs are needed to fix America's trade imbalances.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But there is nothing inherently wrong about running a trade deficit.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It simply means that American consumers are buying more from the world than the world is buying from America.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Moreover, the focus has been solely on the goods trade.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, the US runs a surplus with many of its trading partners in services, exporting software services, education, entertainment, financial and business services.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In Singapore's case, we have a free trade agreement (FTA) with America.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We impose zero tariffs on US imports and we actually run a trade deficit with the US – meaning we buy more from them than they do from us.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But still, we are being subjected to the 10% tariff.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are very disappointed by the US move, especially considering the deep and long-standing friendship between our two countries.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These are not actions one does to a friend.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Asia bears the brunt of the US tariff increase.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Within the region, China is the hardest hit, facing a 34% tariff in this round.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is on top of the 20% tariff increase imposed over the past two months and the 20% from the first Trump administration.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In Southeast Asia, the tariff rates range from 10% to 49%.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These measures will accelerate the fracturing of the global economy.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Instead of flowing based on economic efficiency, capital and trade will increasingly be diverted based on political alignment and security considerations.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Several Members have asked about the impact of the tariffs on specific industries in Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But our deeper worry is not the direct impact that these businesses face.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is the wider implications for the global trading system and the world economy.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, the "reciprocal" tariffs are a fundamental rejection of the WTO rules.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: One of the cornerstones of the WTO multilateral trading system is the Most Favoured Nation (MFN) principle.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Most Favoured Nation sounds like giving special privileges.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Actually, it means the opposite – that every member must treat all other members equally.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In other words, if a country extends more favourable terms or imposes additional restrictions to one trading partner, it must do the same to all other WTO members.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There are some carve-outs and exceptions to the MFN rule, for example, to allow FTAs.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But MFN has long been the bedrock of the multilateral trading system.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It ensures a level playing field, prevents discrimination and enables countries, big and small, to compete fairly in global markets.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This has helped to liberalise trade amongst more than 100 WTO members, each with different economic and political and social concerns.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It opens the door to selective country-by-country trade relationships, based on unilateral preferences.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If other countries adopt the same approach as the US, the rules-based trading system will unravel.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But smaller countries, like Singapore, will face more pressures because small countries have very limited bargaining power in one-on-one bilateral negotiations.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, the major powers will dictate the terms and we risk being marginalised and sidelined.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, the likelihood of a full-blown global trade war is growing.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But other countries may not be guided by the same considerations and may have different perceptions and views.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: China has already imposed retaliatory tariffs on US goods.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Others, like the European Union, are considering their next steps.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some think that the new tariffs are a negotiating tactic, a negotiating tool by the US to extract concessions in other areas.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This was what President Richard Nixon did in 1971.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: He slapped a 10% surcharge on imports to pressure Germany and Japan to devalue their currencies and when they did, the tariffs came off.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, there is a brief window for countries to negotiate and get some reprieve from the US before their higher tariff rates take effect and it may be possible for some rates to be lowered.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Once trade barriers go up, they tend to stay up.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Rolling them back is much harder, even after the original rationale no longer applies.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Even if some partial accommodations are eventually worked out, the uncertainty generated by such a drastic move will dampen global confidence and growth.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This seems to be the fixed minimum tariff, regardless of a country's trade balance or existing trade arrangements.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Furthermore, there are other forces that could maintain the momentum for tariffs.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In particular, many European countries are eager to protect their critical industries, like electric vehicles (EVs), green technologies and semi-conductors, from Chinese competition.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They do not want to become a dumping ground for exports from China or other countries.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There is also a growing push across the West to strengthen their domestic manufacturing capabilities and to reduce dependence on global supply chains, especially in strategic industries.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, this round of tariff increases by the US may just be the beginning of more increases to come globally.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we have seen this play out before.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The US enacted sweeping tariff increases through the Smoot-Hawley Act in 1930.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many countries protested and a number retaliated with their own trade restrictions and tariffs.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In some ways, today's risks may be greater.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The new US tariffs, if fully enacted, are higher than the ones in Smoot-Hawley.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Trade is now a much bigger part of the American and global economy compared to the 1930s.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Supply chains are also more deeply interconnected than they were back then.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Any disruption to trade flows will have wider knock-on effects on the world.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This brings me to the third point, which is the impact on the global economy.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Business and consumer confidence has already been hit by the tariffs.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our economic agencies got in touch with several multinational enterprises (MNEs) and local businesses after the tariff announcement.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Even those who are not directly affected by the tariffs are worried about weakening demand from their consumers.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some have put new projects on hold while they assess the full implications of the tariffs.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But I am sure similar conversations are happening in board rooms elsewhere.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Over the recent days, we have seen sharp negative reactions in global stock markets.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is too early to tell is all these will spill over into the real economy.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: What is troubling is not just the tariffs themselves, which are already damaging, but the fact that this new wave of protectionism is unpredictable and unstable.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many are holding back, fearful that changing rules will leave them with stranded assets.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And all these create an environment of deep uncertainty, one that could tip both the US and the global economy into recession.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: More and more countries are turning away from win-win cooperation and deeper integration.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Instead, we see a rising "me first", win-lose mindset, where it is every country for itself.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some are even prepared to use aggressive or coercive means to get what they want at the expense of others.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Meanwhile, global institutions are getting weaker and long-standing norms of cooperation are breaking down.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: America views China as a strategic competitor and threat, which must be dealt with now while America still has the advantage.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: China says it is ready for a tariff war, a trade war or any other type of war.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There are fewer channels for dialogue, which can serve as guardrails to manage the relationship.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, if the disputes escalate and destabilise US-China relations, the consequences for the world would be disastrous.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The predictable and rules-based order we once knew is fading.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The new era will be more volatile, with more frequent and unpredictable shocks.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We must be ready to stand firm and protect our interests, no matter how the external winds may blow.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The outward-oriented sectors of our economy will suffer the brunt of the impact.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They include, manufacturing, especially segments like electronic and semi-conductors; biomedical science, which have higher exposure to the US; wholesale trade; and transport – these will be impacted.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The global uncertainty and dampened sentiments will also impact some services industries, including finance and insurance.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Singapore may or may not go into recession this year.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Slower growth will mean fewer job opportunities and smaller wage increases for workers.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And if more companies face difficulties or relocate their operations back to the US, there will be higher retrenchments and job losses.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For now, the measures announced in this year's Budget will provide support for any short-term strain.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have a comprehensive package of measures for households and individuals.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They will receive the Community Development Council (CDC) Vouchers, SG60 Vouchers and U-Save rebates to help with their cost of living.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And there are also targeted measures, like increased ComCare Assistance, for the more vulnerable groups.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are also supporting workers through investments in SkillsFuture.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And those who find themselves involuntarily unemployed will receive help to get back on their feet through the SkillsFuture Jobseeker Support scheme which will start later this month.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have also rolled out various measures in the Budget to help businesses.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There are short-term support measures through corporate income tax rebates, as well as schemes to boost their productivity and competitiveness, and to pivot to new markets.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our economic agencies are also engaging the firms impacted by the tariffs to better understand their responses and see how we can support them and assist them with any specific issues they face.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In addition to our economic agencies, the task force will include the Singapore Business Federation, the Singapore National Employers Federation and the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC).

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Government stands ready to do more, if and when necessary.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have the resources to do so because of the financial discipline and prudence we have exercised over the decades.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In this new environment, Singapore must redouble our efforts to remain a key node in global flows and a trusted business hub.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will forge closer ties with like-minded partners who share our commitment to open and free trade.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The US may have decided to turn protectionist, but the rest of the world does not have to follow the same path.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will identify other partners to join us and work around this, to ensure resilience and maintain critical parts of the multilateral system, while laying the foundations for a possible new and different global system that can be achievable later.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And this is why I have made the effort to engage and visit my counterparts in different countries.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I touched base with the United Kingdom's Prime Minister Keir Starmer yesterday and have a few more conversations lined up in the coming weeks.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They are all keen to do more with Singapore and to expand our economic cooperation, including in new areas in the digital and green economies.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In particular, we will strengthen our collaboration and integration within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Last Friday, I spoke with the Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Malaysia is also the ASEAN Chair this year.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We agreed to accelerate ASEAN's integration efforts to make our region more attractive and competitive.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They will discuss further ways that ASEAN can work together to strengthen intra-ASEAN Trade and to send a strong signal of ASEAN's commitment to regional economic integration.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As a group, ASEAN will also continue to strengthen our links with like-minded partners in areas of mutual interest.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The only way Singapore can make it through the gathering storm is to stay united, pool our resources, our resilience and our resolve.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Government will do everything we can to steer Singapore through the choppy waters and make sure no one is left behind.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will keep our economy open, our society cohesive and our institutions strong.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will create new value propositions for businesses and investors.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will act boldly and decisively, when needed, to ensure Singapore continues to succeed.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Above all, we will put the interests of Singapore and Singaporeans at the centre of everything we do.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The dangers are real, but so, too, is our determination.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, Mr Speaker, I say to this House and to fellow Singaporeans: do not fear.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Now, more than ever, we will stay resolute and united.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our little red dot will continue to shine.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I refer to that video message and the Prime Minister's Statement today that referenced vigilance and building up capabilities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even though I accept it is early days and there are a lot of moving parts at the moment and how world economies are assessing their own positions and pivoting to a new reality, there have been references to de-risking and decoupling that have been in the global economy lexicon for some years now.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would be grateful if the Prime Minister could share, when he refers to building up capabilities, is the Prime Minister looking at improving local consumption, notwithstanding our small market, and measures to boost productivity?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Earlier on during Parliamentary Questions, the Senior Minister of State for Manpower suggested that companies should reduce their reliance on cheap foreign labour, do we foresee major structural changes in the way the Singapore economy is shaped, to deal with the new future that we see, which, in the Prime Minister's words, is far more unpredictable than before?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is because we have, over many decades, exercised discipline and prudence in managing our resources, and that is why in these difficult times we are able to put in place the resources to build up the necessary capabilities to see us through the storms ahead.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the task force, I may also ask Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong to say a little bit more later.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But certainly, we are going to engage industries.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will continue the review and the monitoring of the global situation and if there is a need, we will provide further updates to Singaporeans as and when we are ready, and as and when there is a need to.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Perhaps the Deputy Prime Minister Gan can elaborate.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are still working out the detailed composition as well as the tasks forward.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But one of the key focus of the task force is going to be in terms of communication and information sharing.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will be engaging the private sector, so that is why the Prime Minister announced that the composition will include private sector representatives.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The idea is to gather information from the ground, understand the challenges that are faced by the enterprises on the ground and to also discuss with them how we can lean forward to support them, to help them navigate through these uncharted waters as we move ahead under this new landscape.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We also will include union representatives, because we do expect that jobs may be affected.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: And I think, as the Prime Minister emphasised, the focus on training is always the key to our transformation journey and therefore, unions and employers and enterprises will play a key role.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As I said many times before, our main guiding principle is really to be as transparent as possible.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: When we know something important, we will share with the population, with the businesses, with the workers, with the unions and with Members.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: And when we do not know it yet, we will tell you, honestly, that we do not have the information yet.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: So, I think, this is still the early days, as the Leader of the Opposition has also acknowledged.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before we proceed, I would just like to take this opportunity to remind Members that pursuant to Standing Order 23, Members may seek clarifications on the Ministerial Statement, but no debate should be allowed thereon.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members can certainly seek clarifications by way of asking questions, so I seek Members' understanding to keep your clarifications clear and concise.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, can I ask the Prime Minister whether we continue to have access to the key administration officials in the US to negotiate on tariffs?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And where can we land with these discussions, these negotiations?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And also, whether the other initiatives that we are working on, for example, in the military, in the energy space, are these going to be affected by this increase in the tariffs?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The second question to the Prime Minister is, if we, indeed, do trade less with the US because of the tariffs, can I ask where else, and what other markets and corridors can we go to make up for it?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, in the other groupings like the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), ASEAN and so on, and the European Union, are there new corridors, new markets where we can develop more trade relations?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Of course, if the US decides that the baseline rate is universal across all countries, then it is a different consideration altogether, it is not bilateral.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the other aspects of our overall relationship with America, they continue to be important.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In areas, like security and defence, we have such a close relationship built up over many decades and we will continue to maintain that; and we will also discuss cooperation in new areas, like critical new technologies, as well as energy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, these areas of cooperation remain and we certainly want to continue advancing them as well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, structurally, we are in for a more difficult ride, not to mention that if economic activities are going to be configured in a way that is not so much based on efficiency, but security, geopolitical and political considerations, then cost will be higher and at the end of the day, the world ends up operating on a higher cost base.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, these are the harsh realities that we have to be prepared for.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Given that many local businesses operate within global supply chains, how will the anticipated pass-through effect of increased cost to Singapore consumers look like?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And two, for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) that lack the skill to absorb the sudden cost increase, what tailored support is the Ministry considering to ensure that it will remain competitive and can continue to meet consumer demand without raising prices significantly?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I assume this is something that Deputy Prime Minister Gan's task force will look into.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mr Lawrence Wong: Sir, in the near term, if global demand slows down, it may actually mean less inflationary pressures, because global demand is coming off.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is the reason why you see oil prices coming off in the near term.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But as I mentioned just now in my response to Mr Liang Eng Hwa, overall, if the entire global economy is going to be configured on a less efficient basis, it must mean higher cost; and this will impact Singaporeans as well, so we are watching for that and we will continue to monitor that closely.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The impact on Singaporeans, the impact on business and as the Member Mr Yip said, what additional measures may be needed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The first is on international trade and the other is on domestic economic policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I understand that this may mean greater difficulty in arriving at a consensus position, especially with harder hit economies like Vietnam, potentially lowering the common denominator, but at the same time, it greatly strengthens our bargaining position as an economic entity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: ASEAN, for example, is the world's fifth largest economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For the domestic economy, beyond the existing slate of vouchers, I wonder what other policies the Government will be considering in order to shore up consumer demand and to help rebalance the economy toward domestically-driven demand, at least in the short run.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I understand that our small domestic market will never be sufficient alone as a driver of growth, but some short-run stabilisation, I feel, may be valuable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And then, finally, has the Minister also considered the possibility of anti-dumping procedures that may be enacted if, indeed, nations with surpluses choose to export at low prices to Singapore?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And subsequently, we can then share with Members what is the outcome of the discussion.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The idea is to come together to share our information, our assessment of the situation and to explore ways that we can work together moving forward, including discussions with the US, as well as how to further strengthen and deepen regional integration, which will be helpful to our economies as well.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In terms of domestic demand, I should just sound a word of caution that if we are over-stimulating demand, we will end up with inflationary pressures.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, it is something that we have to always be careful about.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And as Assoc Prof Lim pointed out, we have a very small economy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It will not be able to move the needle.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, I think, we just have to bear that in mind.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Usually, anti-dumping duties are introduced in order to protect local, domestic industries that are facing the onslaught of imported products at very low prices, and this is to balance the trade between imports and our local production.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But if our industries are competitive and in fact, they are mostly export-oriented; therefore, I think we have to be very careful in considering introducing anti-dumping duties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are rightly worried about growth issues, loss of jobs and cost of living, but they have also expressed confidence that the People's Action Party Government will stay us through these difficult times.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can we continue to prevent anti-foreigner sentiments from setting in, especially during such times?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, in the near term, whatever issues there are, whatever information the Government has, we will share with the unions, with the businesses, with workers through the task force and other mechanisms.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If there are specific concerns, we will try our best to deal with them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And if we feel that the Budget measures we have or existing measures are not adequate, we will certainly be ready to introduce new measures.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think it is that spirit of working together which has enabled us to overcome previous crises and it will enable us to get through the current difficulties as well.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Mark Lee1,2, I know you had filed Parliamentary Questions on this.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The Prime Minister has rightly pointed out that global conditions are turning increasingly uncertain and many businesses are now bracing for a downturn.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I just want to highlight three key concerns that have surfaced in recent engagements before my supplementary question.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The first is that there is a clear anticipation of a drop in global demand.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Some US-based consumer brands are already advising their supply chain partners to prepare for a mid-term volume reduction of up to 30%.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Long term, no one knows for certain; and this will have a ripple effect on Singapore-based companies.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Second, Singapore businesses are facing margin erosion, especially with clients requesting their supply chain partners to absorb part of the cost shock from the new tariffs because these tariffs are too large to pass through via pricing adjustments in the short term.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This will hit cash flow for our businesses.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: And third, Singapore firms have adopted a "China plus one" strategy investing in Vietnam, Cambodia and Indonesia but now, they are even hit with tariffs higher than the baseline of 10%.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: So, these companies are now under renewed pressure to diversify further, adding another base to stay competitive and it is costly and complex.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I hope Deputy Prime Minister Gan's task force will be looking at the near-term support and would like to clarify if this support will include measures to help Singapore companies in cash flow, relocating or reshoring their supply chains, as well as taking a longer-term view to seize new opportunities arising from these global supply chain shifts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have heard similar feedback amongst our businesses.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not just businesses based in Singapore who are impacted because, as Mr Lee says, some businesses have diversified, expanded and built factories in places like Vietnam, China, and now they are hit with even higher tariffs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And so, it will have impact on their operations and in the end, all this will spill over and impact growth this year and also our prospects for future growth.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Hazel Poa, earlier on, you had raised your hand.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I wanted to call on Members who had raised their hands earlier.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But if it is no longer the case, Mr Saktiandi Supaat.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One is whether the Prime Minister can share with us a bit more about his negotiations within ASEAN, because the Prime Minister mentioned that he had a chat with the Prime Minister of Malaysia, and how the ASEAN negotiations would go ahead in terms of dispute resolution or in terms of the trade tariffs that have been introduced.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, I know the situation is still fluid, but there are concerns about the semi-conductor tariffs that might come onstream.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given that Singapore is a re-export hub, semi-conductor is a significant proportion of our manufacturing sector, can the Prime Minister or Deputy Prime Minister Gan share, on a sectoral basis, the impact of the semi-conductor tariffs, if they do come in, its impact on jobs and GDP in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And the last clarification is whether the Prime Minister or Deputy Prime Minister Gan can share, at the interim and at the start, whether there has been macro counterfactual simulations of existing tariffs that have been introduced and whether if there is an addition of 5% or 10% tariffs or semi-conductor tariffs, the impact on growth and jobs for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I think I will give the Member a very broad assessment of the impacts, as I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I think we still need to look at what the US is going to do with regard to semi-conductors.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is indeed something that is of great concern to us.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have been engaging the semi-conductor companies and to discuss with them what we can do to help them to make sure that they are able to manage the impact of the import duties.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is something that we will continue to have to work with them and see how we can manage the potential impact of duties on Singapore's exports to the US.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the first question about negotiations and whether we are going to do this bilaterally or collectively as ASEAN, I think the ASEAN member states, each one of us, bilaterally will already engage America – we will certainly do so and I am sure other countries are doing so as well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Member would have read that about that in the media.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: ASEAN's tariffs are already largely removed, but to reduce further non-tariff barriers, to facilitate better trade within ASEAN and to ensure that ASEAN remains even more attractive and competitive, I think those are actions that we certainly want to do.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a nation, we have a good track record of overcoming challenges like the oil crisis, the Asian Financial Crisis, SARS and COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The tariffs are game-changing, but we do not know 100% the long-term economic impact on Singapore at this moment.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First question, as Singapore has the lowest 10% tariff in Asia, does the Government not believe that this will put us in a stronger competitive position to continue exporting to the US?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second clarification, what are the chances that these tariffs will be temporary, perhaps not more than two years?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Three, does the Prime Minister believe that the world has been adjusting to a post-Pax Americana era for a while, and this move by the Trump Administration will only accelerate this process and the world may arrive at a new equilibrium sooner?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fourth and last clarification, Singapore is now a far larger economy and diverse society than before.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Prime Minister agree that the right approach to dealing with adversity is to have free contestation of ideas and not group think?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And the Government will continue to engage all stakeholders to build a better future for everyone in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the questions that Mr Leong raised, in fact, some of them were already addressed in my speech.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I did say that today's order is eroding and a new order is coming in place.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And indeed, America's actions may accelerate this move.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we are in a period of transition, one that is uncertain, unsettled and increasingly unstable.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Transitions are always unstable until you eventually find a new equilibrium – and we have no idea what that new equilibrium will be or when we will get there.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I also mentioned this in my speech just now.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are some hopes that the negotiations may bring down the higher tariffs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I think we have to be realistic, not sure that this can be done.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are not going back to the previous status quo.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are in a new phase with higher trade barriers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Should we take comfort that we are in the lowest tier?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Well, I suppose if you want to see silver linings in dark clouds, you can say so.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But certainly, for us as a country, so reliant on trade for our growth, on external markets for our living, this new environment will be detrimental to Singapore's longer-term prospects.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, I take no comfort at all in us being in the lowest tier and I think that we have to brace ourselves for a much bumpier ride ahead.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The current US administration seems to have shown themselves to be fairly open to bilateral negotiations and in fact, has encouraged bilateral negotiations.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: For small countries like ourselves, it is obviously a lot harder to negotiate because the negotiation is not done on the basis of any straight international law but more of the laws of the jungle, which is, what can you do for me today?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: From a perception standpoint, certainly, in the US and perceptions shared by many senior folks in the current administration, Singapore is seen as a rich country with significant, not natural but financial resources, especially in the three sovereign wealth funds, or two plus one, our sovereign wealth system.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I fully appreciate this is a hypothetical question, but the view is, if down the road, in a negotiation, we are asked, "What can you give to us?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Can you commit a $100 billion commitment to invest in US manufacturing to create x-number of jobs?", how will we respond to that as a country, keeping in mind that our sovereign wealth funds are managed absolutely independently?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The second point is more regarding the domestic companies that we have in Singapore, whose margins have been shrinking even prior to this latest sell war.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the second question on supporting companies, again, we have gone through that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We understand that there will be an impact on our local businesses.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will engage them more, understand better how exactly they are affected by the tariffs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: A lot of this is still evolving, as many Members recognise.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And so, as we get better information, as we drill down into some of the details, we will be in a better position to shape our responses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Speaker, I would like to thank the Prime Minister for his assuring words on the uncertainty that is facing us today.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Has there been any indication of a slowdown or withdrawal of foreign investments in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: My second clarification is, in light of the evolving global order or the transition, as the Prime Minister has mentioned, while we appreciate the grants and support measures to assist our companies and our workforce, how can Singapore adopt a more proactive stance in navigating this era of uncertainly?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we find the opportunities in these troubled waters?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What role can we play, especially in the global world order, and what unique value propositions can we offer to remain relevant and contribute meaningfully to this global economic transition?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We hope this will continue to be the case, but it is still early days.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will continue to engage the key MNEs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why the concern is not just about tariffs alone, damaging though they are, but the wider uncertainty about potential changes in rules, which is causing companies everywhere to hold back on new projects, hold back on taking decisions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: All that can easily tip the world into a slowdown.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On opportunities, Sir, I highlighted we are engaging our countries in ASEAN to see what more we can do as ASEAN to make ASEAN more competitive.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is renewed, I would say, emphasis and a strong desire to do more, particularly in this new environment.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we are hopeful that we can push through some of these ASEAN initiatives.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are other like-minded countries who believe firmly in a rules-based trading system, in open and free trade.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are in touch with them, engaging them to see what more we can do together.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are will be a coalition of like-minded countries which we will be amongst them, identifying new opportunities for ourselves, finding ways to retain key elements of the multilateral system and seeing how we can evolve and shape a better global system together.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Prime Minister just now acknowledged that this was a silver lining.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But are our economic agencies stepping up efforts to help Singapore firms secure US demand in these areas before global buyers reorganise their supply chains and lock in new sourcing arrangements?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At some point in time, you will find that we are also going to face challenges as well.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, we have to exercise some care in organising this, but certainly, we will continue to explore.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Also bear in mind that unless we are in the same market, some of the components that we purchase will then become more expensive because they are going to face duties.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But at the same time, some of the economies that are selling our products to may be exporting to the US.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If they are facing a higher tariff from the US, then our exports may be affected because, then their demand will come down; they will buy less from us.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I think this is an entire global chain effect.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We should not look at it just simply from any particular single segment of the trade because it is going to change the entire playing field.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, that is why the Prime Minister mentioned that this is going to be a new economic landscape that we need to appreciate, to understand how it is going to be reorganised and restructured.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: One of the purposes of the task force is to engage the private sector, to engage the people on the ground who are operating this and to have a sense of where they are moving their pieces.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Are they going to relocate their production base?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Are they going to change their purchasing strategy?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Where the products are going to come from and where our exports are going to?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: All these, we need to have a better assessment.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: All these are in a flux today because everyone is still negotiating and they are still thinking through what they need to do.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Particularly, in semi-conductor, it is a very complex supply chain.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If you move one piece, you need to move the entire ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, it is not so easy to adjust and to reconfigure the semi-conductor ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I agree with this point but my worry is about global leadership for and from the rest of the world to double down on this integration going forward.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, what is the Prime Minister's assessment of how the void in global leadership, left behind by the US, can be filled; and also how may Singapore contribute to and support this backfilling in the global leadership void?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is precisely why there is so much uncertainty in the world today.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Who is going to step into the vacuum?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These are efforts that we will continue to press on.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If I may be allowed to explain what happened earlier.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I did have questions, but as clarification was going on, I was revising my questions and you caught me —

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Given that we are a small country, are we exploring joint negotiations with other countries?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I believe there are enough common interest for this to be feasible.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I also wish to note that I am glad to hear that the Government is trying to convert this challenge into an impetus to push for free trade with the rest of the world.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I wish to convey my best wishes to the task force led by the Deputy Prime Minister Gan.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But there are exceptions that are granted under the FTA for emergency economic situations.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And therefore, they are going under that provision to say, "we have the right to introduce that".

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Of course, for parties to the FTA, you also have the right to challenge the assumption.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And therefore, you go into a consultation, dispute resolution and to see how we can address the issue, whether first and foremost it is an economic emergency that entitles them to invoke that provision.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, that is the technical part of the provision under the FTA.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: What we are doing now is, we are, first, going to embark on a consultation to work with them, to engage them, to first understand what their concerns are that caused them to introduce this basic tariff rate.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And therefore, I think we will just continue to focus on engaging with the US to find out what are their concerns, whether we are able to address their concerns, so as to, hopefully, as the Prime Minister said, if there is room to negotiate, we will see whether we can negotiate for a lowered or waiver of the import tariffs on Singapore's exports to the US.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But even if that is not possible, it is also useful for us to have this engagement to prevent further escalation of import duties, import tariffs on Singapore's exports.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As the Member know, they are still in a flux and tariffs that we see today are not the final duties, and there could be additional duties, tariffs that could be imposed.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, I think it is very useful for us to continue this engagement.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I think the Member also earlier talked about whether we are looking at joining hands with our ASEAN partners to see how we can engage the US together, collectively.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My question is, how will our Government communicate to younger people in Singapore from here onwards?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I was only in my mid-20s and working in the banking sector during the Asian Financial Crisis, when I experienced treasury profits, hard-earned over months, wiped out in days.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And I was in my mid-30s when I was working in the social service sector and saw how corporates who had been supporting us, charities or the lower-income, with donations and volunteers, had to roll out very painful retrenchment programmes to keep the companies afloat and keep as many jobs as they can.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, my question to the Prime Minister is, our youths as young as 18 years to maybe 35 years from my Youth Network (YN) shared with me that they really benefited from the Prime Minister's engagement with them through the YN platform; so, how will we engage them to help them understand what is going to come going forward and go through the hard ride?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we will not just stop at putting out clips on social media or discussing this in Parliament because we are facing real threats, real dangers that all Singaporeans should be aware of.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And so, beyond discussing these issues in this House and sharing them on social media, we will be engaging different engagement sessions with young people, with Singaporeans from different segments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We do that each time we encounter threats, dangers or deal with a crisis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have done that during COVID-19 when we had to repeatedly engage Singaporeans to address the concerns and to help them understand the nature of the threat and how we are to respond.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In the same way now, when we are dealing with a new situation that poses very real economic threats to our livelihoods and jobs, we will do the same in engaging Singaporeans, young and old.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Any more clarifications for the Prime Minister or Deputy Prime Minister Gan?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: End of the Ministerial Statement by the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will now move on to the next Ministerial Statement.
